transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, I came in because... I just can't stop thinking about how the left side of my face looks. It just looks off to me. Like, my nose and my jaw, they look crooked. I see it in every ID photo, and whenever I have to turn my camera on for online classes, it's right there. People tell me they don't see it, but... I feel like everyone in the CNC lab is noticing it. Like they're looking at my crooked face before they even look at my work. It's just really getting to me.
How much time per day would you say you spend thinking about or checking how your face looks?

It's hard to give an exact number of hours, but it takes up a huge part of my day. Mostly before I leave for school... I just get stuck. I'll be in the bathroom checking my face in the mirror, and then I use my phone camera to check it again. I spend a lot of time fixing my hair or changing my shirts to try and hide the angle. I even keep asking my mom if it looks weird. Sometimes I'm doing all this for so long that I actually miss my lab completely. Or if I do make it, I show up too wiped out to even focus on anything.

latest_inference.note: Patient demonstrates body dysmorphic disorder criteria: preoccupation with perceived facial defect (nose, jaw asymmetry), repetitive behaviors (mirror checking, camera checking, reassurance seeking), significant time consumption (hours daily, missing classes), functional impairment (missing lab, showing up exhausted). This rules out F48.1 (neurasthenia - lacks the body image focus), F41.1 (generalized anxiety - too specific to appearance), and F40.00 (agoraphobia - not the primary presentation).

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with Body Dysmorphic Disorder (F45.21), characterized by preoccupation with a perceived defect in physical appearance (asymmetry of facial features) that is not observable or appears slight to others. The preoccupation consumes significant time daily (mirror checking, photo checking, reassurance-seeking, appearance-focused behaviors), causes marked distress, and results in functional impairment (missing classes, inability to concentrate in lab). Repetitive behaviors (mirror checking, camera checking, reassurance-seeking, outfit changing) are present. The symptoms meet criteria for BDD with insight being poor (patient believes others are noticing despite reassurance).
